The head of the World Health Organization this week warned that the current outbreak threatens to be the biggest ever, with authorities playing catch-up to the disease after “ a big head start. ” During the previous deadliest outbreak, which killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016, authorities had recorded 755 cases at the same point . — Jeronimo Gonzalez

stories.summary: Thursday's edition of The New York Times asked a question I've been asking here for over a decade: "Is Letting Children Out Alone A Rite of Passage or a Crime?" Reason readers know it can, in some sense, be both: a rite of passage too often treated as a crime. One of the primary missions of Let Grow , the nonprofit I cofounded, is to make sure the parents who trust their kids with some reasonable independence are not investigated for neglect. But they are. articles.summary: Three adolescent boys are gathered in a ramshackle tree house—the kind you might have built yourself as a kid, if you were born before 1990, using scrap wood and a bucket of nails; the kind that would get you an unpleasant visit from your homeowners association were your own kids to attempt the same thing today. articles.summary: The recently confirmed $1.5 billion Bartz v. Anthropic settlement, in which the AI behemoth agreed to pay to compensate authors whose copyrighted works it had scraped for use in training large language models (LLMs), was widely painted in the press as a win for individual authors and media industries in general. President and CEO of the Association of American Publishers Maria Pallante issued a statement celebrating what she called “an important victory in the larger battle to hold big tech accountable for its unscrupulous appropriation of intellectual and creative properties that clearly belong to authors and publishers.”  Anthropic will make this one-time payment to authors and publishers whose works the company clearly lifted from pirate sites, retained, and replicated in their training data; 482,460 works were eligible, and the split is currently estimated at about $3,000 per title, shared evenly between author and publisher. While the entire payment was initially supposed to go to authors, publishers successfully fought for half.
